topics.title: The Cold War: Definition and Outbreak (Ideological Differences)
topics.notesHtml:
The Cold War

The end of the Second World War led to a decisive change in the power balance around the world. Countries that had previously dominated European affairs, such as France, Britain and Germany, were now poorer or less powerful. World history was much more affected by what the leaders of the new 'superpowers' believed and did (USA and USSR). From entering Berlin together and celebrating VE Day, relations between the two superpowers deteriorated in the succeeding years, leading to decades of geopolitical conflict and rivalry known as the Cold War.

Definition

In a traditional sense, the Cold War is not considered an actual war where direct and actual fighting takes place. Rather, it can be classified as a state of hostility and high tensions where conflict takes the form of non-cooperation, including propaganda from both sides and economic measures.

The Cold War can be divided into 3 phases:

  • Outbreak
  • Escalation
  • Manifestation

1. Outbreak of the Cold War

How did the Cold War start? How did the USA and USSR turn from allies to enemies?

a) Ideological Differences/Conflict

Although the USA and USSR were wartime allies, they inherently believed in differing ideologies, political and economic systems. This difference of beliefs laid the basis of all subsequent conflicts during the Cold War.

Capitalism (USA)Communism (USSR)
Distinct class differences → disparity in wealthClassless system → equitable distribution; everyone is equal
Individual enterprises; businesses owned by private individuals. Market economy → production determined by market forces; prices set by competitionState-controlled economy; government owns means of production. Command economy → production determined by state government; prices set by state
Promotes democratic political freedoms (includes freedom of speech/multi-party system elections) → values freedomConcentrates power into the hands of a select few; one-party rule/authoritarian dictatorship → lack of freedom; does not value freedom → possibly corrupt politicians, party officials and government
Healthcare managed by private sectorFree healthcare services
—One-party state (only the Communist Party allowed to contest elections)

As seen from the table above, both systems of governance differ greatly. Communism entailed high levels of government intervention, giving the state a lot of power, while Capitalism believed in individual rights and the value of freedom. This difference led to conflict as both powers attempted to spread their own ideologies to others, gaining influence to try to outmatch each other, causing tension, a rise in hostility and, eventually, the Cold War.

Flow chart depiction

The West follows a capitalist system while the USSR follows a communist system; both ideologies are conflicting.

↓ Both sides believed their system/ideology was better and wanted to spread the influence of their ideologies.

↓ Mistrust and suspicion began to spread between Americans and Soviets.

↓ Soon, both sides were at odds with each other; tensions and hostilities rose, resulting in the Cold War.

topics.title: Breakdown in Wartime Alliance: The Yalta and Potsdam Conferences
topics.notesHtml:
b) Breakdown in Wartime Alliance

When Germany invaded Russia and was pulled to declare war on the USA by Japan, the USSR and USA found themselves in an unlikely alliance, fighting together against a common enemy. After the defeat of Germany in 1945, both celebrated together; however, the problems brought by the war would soon turn relations sour.

In February 1945, as Germany was on the brink of defeat, Allied leaders met at Yalta, Ukraine, to plan what would happen after Germany's defeat. The Yalta Conference went well. Despite their differences, the Big Three — Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill — agreed on some important matters. It seemed that, although they couldn't all agree, they were still able to negotiate and do business with one another.

Yalta Conference (February 1945)

AgreementsDisagreements
On Japan: Stalin agreed to enter the war against Japan once Germany surrendered.On Borders: Stalin wanted the border of the USSR to move westward into Poland, much to the disapproval of Roosevelt and Churchill.
On the United Nations: The Big Three agreed to the new United Nations, successor of the League of Nations, to keep peace after the war.On Elections: The Declaration of Liberated Europe promised that countries liberated from the German army would be allowed to hold free elections regarding their government.
On Germany: The Big Three agreed that Germany would be divided into 4 zones: American, British, French and Soviet.On Poland: A government of 'national security' was to be set up in Poland, comprising both communists and non-communists.

Post-Yalta Changes

  • Stalin's armies were occupying most of Eastern Europe: Soviet troops had liberated country after country in Eastern Europe, but instead of withdrawing his troops, Stalin left them there. Refugees were fleeing the country, fearing a communist takeover. Stalin had set up a communist government in Poland, ignoring the wishes of the majority of the Poles. He insisted his control of Eastern Europe was a defensive measure against possible future attacks.
  • America had a new president: President Roosevelt died on 12 April 1945 and was succeeded by his vice president, Harry Truman. Truman was much more anticommunist than Roosevelt and was very suspicious of Stalin; together with his advisors, he saw Soviet actions in Eastern Europe as preparations for a Soviet takeover of the rest of Europe.
  • The Allies had tested an atomic bomb: On 16 July 1945, the Allies successfully tested an atomic bomb at a desert site in the USA, completing the Manhattan Project. At the start of the Potsdam Conference, Truman informed Stalin about it.

In July 1945, after the relative success of the Yalta Conference and the defeat of Germany (in May), Allied leaders met at Potsdam, Germany, to decide on the administration of Germany. The Potsdam Conference went less than ideally. The Big Three were not able to come up with any new agreements, and most agreements at Potsdam had already been decided at Yalta. There were many disagreements between the leaders, and they left displeased and angry, causing hostilities between the Allies and the USSR to increase.

Potsdam Conference (July 1945)

AgreementsDisagreements
On Post-War Europe: A Council of Foreign Ministers was to be set up. Military administration of Germany was established.On Borders: Stalin's request to define the Polish-German border was put off till the peace treaty. There were also arguments over where the boundaries between the zones would be drawn.
On the German Economy: The leaders agreed to place primary emphasis on the development of agriculture and non-military industry. Institutions that had controlled the economy under the Nazis were to be decentralized, and all of Germany would be treated as a single economic unit.On Elections: Stalin did not allow free elections in Eastern Europe, and a communist government was being set up in Poland; communists were coming to power in the countries of Eastern Europe.
On War Criminals: War criminals would be brought to trial.On Reparations: There were arguments about how much the USSR should be allowed to take in reparations. Stalin wanted compensation from Germany for the 20 million Russian deaths in the war; Truman was hesitant. It was agreed the Soviets could take whatever they wanted from the Soviet-controlled zone and 10 per cent from the Western zones. This remained a source of disagreement, with the Western Allies worried they were repeating the mistakes of the Treaty of Versailles after World War One, feeling reparations had gone overboard.
On Borders: The conference accepted Stalin's request to transfer the land east of the Oder and Neisse rivers from Germany to Poland.On Poland: Truman was angry because Stalin had arrested the non-communist leaders of Poland.
On Reparations: A compromise was worked out, based on an exchange of capital equipment from the Western zone for raw materials from the East.On Nuclear Arsenal: Truman did not tell Stalin about the development of the nuclear bombs in the US, and Stalin was furious when he finally found out.
—On Germany: Stalin intended to cripple Germany completely in order to protect the USSR against future threats. Truman did not want a repeat of WW2.
—On Eastern Europe: At Yalta, Stalin had won agreement from the Allies that he could set up pro-Soviet governments in Eastern Europe, saying, "if the Slav people are united, no one will dare move a finger against them." Truman became very unhappy with Stalin's intentions and soon adopted a 'get tough' attitude towards Stalin.

shortAnswer.prompt: Compare the outcomes of the Yalta and Potsdam Conferences. How similar or different were the levels of cooperation between the Big Three at each conference?
shortAnswer.modelAnswer: Yalta and Potsdam differ in the level of cooperation achieved. At Yalta, despite some disagreements (e.g. over Poland's borders and elections), the Big Three still reached several agreements, such as on the United Nations and the division of Germany into four zones, showing the wartime alliance was still functioning. In contrast, at Potsdam, the Big Three came up with few new agreements, with most decisions already settled at Yalta, and disagreements over reparations, borders, and Stalin's actions in Poland caused the leaders to leave angry and displeased. This suggests that between Yalta and Potsdam, mutual trust and willingness to cooperate had deteriorated significantly, foreshadowing the Cold War.

shortAnswer.prompt: How useful are the Yalta and Potsdam Conferences as evidence of a breakdown in the wartime alliance between the USA and USSR?
shortAnswer.modelAnswer: The conferences are useful as evidence of a breakdown because they show a clear shift from cooperation at Yalta (agreement on the UN, zones of Germany, Japan) to open disagreement at Potsdam (over reparations, Poland, and the atomic bomb secret), with leaders leaving Potsdam 'displeased and angry'. This is supported by contextual knowledge that Truman, more anticommunist than Roosevelt, adopted a 'get tough' attitude after Potsdam. However, the conferences alone have limitations as evidence: they do not capture broader mutual suspicions rooted in pre-war events (e.g. the Nazi-Soviet Pact, the Manhattan Project's secrecy) which also fuelled distrust independent of the conferences themselves. Thus, while useful in showing the growing rift between the superpowers, the conferences must be read alongside other developments for a fuller picture of the alliance's breakdown.

topics.title: Mistrust and Suspicion; Post-War Developments (Iron Curtain and Eastern Europe)
topics.notesHtml:
c) Mistrust and Suspicion

Actions which drew suspicion and worsened relations between the West and the USSR:

The WestUSSR
1939 Munich Agreement: When negotiating with Hitler over the fate of the Sudetenland, Russia was not invited to the talks. This expressed the West's fear of communism, indicating to Stalin that they were willing to allow Hitler to destroy Russia before taking action. Giving Hitler the Sudetenland, allowing him to advance East, and refusing Russia a voice only furthered distrust. Communism was also seen as a mutual enemy, which motivated the policy of Appeasement. Perceived delays in opening a second front and delayed action after the invasion of the USSR also caused Stalin to lose faith in the Allies, resulting in his post-war feelings of insecurity.1917 Russian Revolution: In 1917, communist ideology led to a revolution which overthrew the Duma provisional government. This event caused fear within the West, as they suspected communism would be a threat to their democratic system of governance, with the potential to disrupt the order of society and topple other forms of government.
1939–46 Manhattan Project: Russia feared the power of America's atomic bomb. The success of the first nuclear arms had shocked and angered Stalin, as its development was kept secret from him. This caused feelings of wariness and suspicion in the USSR about the motives of the West.1939 Nazi-Soviet Pact: In 1939, the USSR signed the Nazi-Soviet Pact (Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact) with Nazi Germany, promising mutual non-aggression and benefit through cooperation. This revealed suspicion between the Allies and the USSR, as they refused to put aside their differences and ally against Hitler, resulting in the USSR deciding the best option was to work with the enemy. It was only after betrayal and dismantling of the pact that the USSR had to align with the Allies for self-preservation.

The disagreements at the Potsdam Conference had soured relations between the US and USSR. This was coupled with various suspicious actions by both sides in WW2, which made them wary of each other. Disparities between both countries increased as the US underwent a leadership transition, with a more anti-communist person helming the country. The situation further escalated as Stalin's army was occupying Eastern Europe while the Americans had developed a nuclear bomb. All these events contributed to heightened tensions and hostility between the two superpowers, with violence being a very real possibility.

Post-War Developments

The WestUSSR
The Iron Curtain (1946): On a visit to Westminster College, Fulton, USA, former British Prime Minister Winston Churchill made a speech, using the term "The Iron Curtain" for the first time to describe the divide of Eastern Europe from Western Europe. The Iron Curtain was created by the Soviet Union after World War II. It stood for an ideological and military barrier between the countries under the dependence of the Soviet Union and the non-communist, politically free countries in the West. Behind the Iron Curtain were included almost all of the states in Central and Eastern Europe. One of its main tasks was to restrict people inhabiting the communist area from travelling outside, and to restrict the information flow into it from the non-communist world. The Iron Curtain strengthened its position during the Cold War, becoming the border that constructed the bipolar structure of world politics. The speech worsened the conflict between the two superpowers, highlighting the imminent dangers of Soviet and communist influence in Europe and galvanising America into action.Eastern Europe: Despite initial agreement at Yalta that Eastern European nations would have free elections for their governments, fear of the West and determination to secure the USSR against Western aggression compelled Stalin to install 'friendly', pro-Moscow Soviet satellite states. By 1945, the Red Army occupied all of Eastern Europe except Albania, Yugoslavia and Greece. By 1948, only Greece did not have a communist government. The West viewed this as expansionist and an attempt to spread communism through world domination. From 1946–47, Stalin made sure Communist governments came to power in all the countries of Eastern Europe (those the Soviet Union had conquered in 1945). The Communist description of this process was 'slicing salami' — gradually getting rid of all opposition, bit by bit.

From Churchill's Iron Curtain speech: "From Stettin in the Baltic to Trieste in the Adriatic an iron curtain has descended across the Continent. Behind that line lie all the capitals of the ancient states of Central and Eastern Europe. Warsaw, Berlin, Prague, Vienna, Budapest, Belgrade, Bucharest and Sofia; all these famous cities and the populations around them lie in what I must call the Soviet sphere, and all are subject, in one form or another, not only to Soviet influence but to a very high and in some cases increasing measure of control from Moscow.... The Russian-dominated Polish government has been encouraged to make enormous and wrongful inroads upon Germany, and mass expulsions of millions of Germans on a scale grievous and undreamed-of are now taking place. The Communist parties, which were very small in all these Eastern States of Europe, have been raised to preeminence and power far beyond their numbers and are seeking everywhere to obtain totalitarian control. Police governments are prevailing in nearly every case, and so far, except in Czechoslovakia, there is no true democracy."

topics.title: Escalation: Greece and Czechoslovakia, the Truman Doctrine, Containment, the Marshall Plan and NATO
topics.notesHtml:
2. Escalation

How did the West react to Stalin's actions?

Greece, 1947

In 1946, a civil war erupted in Greece between the Soviet-backed communists and the British-backed monarchists. Monarchists wanted the return of the king of Greece; communists wanted Greece to be a Soviet Republic. The British could not afford such a war and intended to withdraw their troops, previously sent to Greece to restore order and supervise free elections. Truman intervened: paid for by the Americans, some British troops stayed in Greece and tried to prop up the King's government. By 1950, the royalists were in control of Greece, although they were a very weak government, always in crisis.

Czechoslovakia, 1948

Czechoslovakia was ruled by a coalition government which, although it included communists, had been trying to pursue policies independent of Moscow. The communists retaliated by purging anti-Soviet leaders. A pro-American minister, Jan Masaryk, was found dead below his open window. The communists said he had jumped; the Americans suspected he'd been pushed.

Truman Doctrine

When the Greek Civil War broke out, the Americans were alarmed. Despite the conflict only taking place at a local scale, America viewed it as a threat of communist takeover and subsequent spread. In response, President Truman declared that the United States would provide aid (money, equipment and advice) to any country under the threat of communist takeover. This policy of aid is known as the Truman Doctrine. With it, the Americans exited their isolationist policy and became more involved with European affairs.

Containment Policy

Communism would be limited only to areas already under Soviet control, and Americans would resist Soviet expansion everywhere else. In the late 1940s, the USSR made attempts to extend her influence, by stationing her army in Eastern Europe and installing satellite communist governments there. The USSR also created Cominform, to coordinate the activity between the communist parties in Europe. This raised grave concerns among Americans, and a policy of containment was adopted to stop the spread of communism into other nations. The manifestation of this policy can be seen through the Truman Doctrine, where Americans promised military and economic aid to any country under threat of communist takeover.

Common symbols: Uncle Sam as America; Bear as communism/USSR.

Marshall Plan

After WW2, Western Europe was in ruins. Truman was worried that weakened Western European nations would be more susceptible to communism. He sent Secretary of State and former US Army general George Marshall to assess the economic state of Europe. Europe's economy was ruined — nations owed millions to the US, had extreme shortages of all goods, food, clothing, coal and houses, and had damaged houses and infrastructure left over from the war that needed money to repair. Marshall suggested $17 billion to rebuild Europe's economy, and Truman put this plan to Congress. Only after the events in Czechoslovakia did Congress accept the plan to pay $17 billion over 4 years from 1948.

Views on Aims of the Marshall Plan

WestEast
The Marshall Plan was generous and a great contribution to world peace (partly motivated by self-interest):
  • Prevent Communism: Provides aid to Western European nations, allowing them to recover quickly and prosper. A rich and strong Europe would create stable democratic governments, making communism less attractive to residents of Western Europe and preventing its spread to the rest of the continent.
  • Benefit Economy: A prosperous Western Europe also creates new markets for American goods. The USA had already experienced the effects of the Great Depression, and Truman wanted to prevent another worldwide slump.
The Marshall Plan was a ploy by the USA to exploit Europe and gain power (Stalin was extremely suspicious and refused to have anything to do with it):
  • Spreading American Influence: The anticommunist aims of the plan tried to weaken Stalin's hold on Eastern Europe. Stalin also felt the USA was trying to dominate as many states as possible by making them dependent on the US dollar. Stalin forbade any of the Eastern European satellite states from accepting aid from the US.

"The ruling gang of American imperialists has taken the path of open expansion, of enslaving weakened capitalist countries. It has hatched new war plans against the Soviet Union. Imitating Hitler, the new aggressors are using blackmail." — G.M. Malenkov, a Soviet politician, speaking in 1947 about the Marshall Plan.

In conclusion, the Marshall Plan was created due to: (1) fear of communist takeover of weakened Western Europe, and (2) fear of the loss of a free market for American goods and trade. By 1952, the economies of Western Europe had recovered, and economic growth surpassed pre-war levels. Molotov called this 'dollar imperialism' — an attempt to spread democracy and capitalism through the use of money. As the Marshall Plan went well, with Western European nations recovering, Stalin created Cominform and Comecon in response.

NATO

In the late 1940s, the Allies, particularly America, practised the policy of containment, an effort to prevent any further spread of communism. The USSR's actions alarmed the Allies, especially during the Berlin Blockade, where war seemed a real possibility. The US was not convinced Russia would control her ambitions to further expand into other nations, particularly Western Europe. This fear ultimately resulted in the creation of NATO, the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation, a security alliance between non-communist European nations and the United States and Canada, signed in 1949. Should any nation invade any NATO member state, it would be considered an attack on all NATO member nations, promoting a response from the US and other NATO members to assist the country under attack. This would serve as a deterrent to the USSR from invading any Western European nations and would therefore contain communism.

In essence, NATO is: (1) a security alliance between the US, Canada and non-communist Western European nations; (2) created due to the threat of Soviet expansion.

topics.title: How Stalin Reacted: Cominform, Comecon and the Warsaw Pact
topics.notesHtml:
How did Stalin react to the West's actions?

Cominform

The Cominform (Communist Information Bureau) was created in 1947 to coordinate the activities of Communist Parties in Europe under the direction of the USSR. This was done both in response to Communist leaders in European nations being uncertain of whether they should participate in the Paris Conference on the Marshall Plan, as well as in response to the Marshall Plan itself. It also aimed to tighten Soviet control in Eastern Europe, to build collective heavy industry in those countries, and to create a trade network between Communist countries. It published its own newspaper to spread Communist ideals and held conferences in the Eastern Bloc. Communist leaders also gathered in Moscow to take instruction from Stalin.

Comecon (Council for Mutual Economic Assistance)

Established in 1949 to facilitate and coordinate the economic development, planning and trade of the Eastern European countries belonging to the Soviet bloc.

Warsaw Pact

Created in response to the admission of West Germany as a member state of NATO, partly due to the creation of NATO itself. In 1955, after NATO admitted West Germany as a member, the USSR began to feel the threat of the West, with a security alliance that stretched from the Western European coast all the way to the border of Russia's sphere of influence. In order to protect herself and her satellite communist states, the USSR created the Warsaw Pact, a security alliance similar to NATO, involving several satellite states under communist influence. Similar to NATO, an attack on any member state in the Warsaw Pact would have been considered an attack on all Warsaw Pact nations, prompting a response from all member states to defend the nation under attack. The Warsaw Pact was another piece of evidence of the USSR's threat and the threat of communism.

In essence, the Warsaw Pact was: (1) a security alliance between the USSR and the communist satellite states; (2) created in response to the growing threat and power of the West, after the creation of NATO.

This suggests the USSR was reacting to perceived Western encroachment rather than initiating aggression. However, these bodies also tightened Soviet control over Eastern Europe (e.g. Cominform's role in enforcing Moscow's direction) and coordinated a trade network under Soviet dominance, suggesting an element of consolidating and expanding Soviet influence rather than purely defensive intent. Both alliances also shared the same structural principle, that an attack on one member would be treated as an attack on all, showing that each side essentially mirrored the other's strategy for collective defence. This suggests that the alliances were less about ideology alone and more a direct, almost reactive cycle of mutual security responses between the two superpowers.

topics.title: Division of Germany, Bizonia, and the Berlin Blockade/Airlift
topics.notesHtml:
Division of Germany, Bizonia and the Berlin Blockade

After the war, it was agreed for Germany to be divided into 4 zones. Initially, Truman intended to remove all German industry and make it an agricultural country so it could never wage war again. However, growing concerns over the USSR made Truman decide that a strong Germany might be a useful ally. It was also clear that if German industries were not allowed to recover, millions would starve.

In 1947, America and Britain combined their zones into Bizonia, and with the addition of France in 1948, the entity became known as the Trizone (West Germany).

Stalin believed Germany should be kept poor and weak, to prevent it from being a threat to European powers again. Stalin also wanted reparations for damage done to the USSR and began to exact this from its zone. 10 million refugees fled from the Soviet zone to other Western-powers-occupied zones, straining resources on the Western powers.

In order to help the West German economy recover, the Allies agreed to create a new currency, the Deutsche Mark, replacing the severely inflated old currency. Bizonia began receiving aid under the Marshall Plan, and Western zones began to recover and prosper. Stalin felt he had to show Western leaders that he would fight back if they encroached on the Soviet 'Sphere of Influence'. Afraid that Germany would grow strong and threaten the USSR, Stalin planned to seize control of West Berlin through a blockade, hoping to force the Western powers to leave the city by blocking all supplies of food to West Berlin.

West Berlin lay deep in the Soviet zone and was connected to the West via roads, railways and canals which crossed Soviet territory, much to Stalin's resentment. In 1948, Stalin blocked these supply lines, stopping the Western powers from reaching their zones in Berlin. He aimed to starve the people of West Berlin until they surrendered to communist rule. If the USA rammed roadblocks or railway blocks, it would be seen as an act of war. Stalin expected Truman to announce an embarrassing withdrawal from Berlin, giving him Soviet control of the entire city and a propaganda victory.

Berlin Airlift

The West had three options: (1) break down and ram the blockade, potentially initiating a war with the USSR and being blamed as the aggressor; (2) give in to Stalin's demands and withdraw from Berlin, suffering an embarrassing defeat and paving the way for the entire Germany to fall to the USSR; or (3) find another method to deliver food and supplies.

Unsurprisingly, they chose the third option. From June 1948 to May 1949, US and British planes airlifted 1.5 million tons of supplies to the residents of West Berlin. This was an extremely risky move, as if the USSR had shot the planes, war would have started between both nations. No shots were fired, and for the next 10 months, West Berlin received all their supplies this way — everything from food, clothing, building materials and oil. After 200,000 flights, the Soviet Union finally lifted the blockade.

topics.title: Manifestation of the Cold War and the Korean War
topics.notesHtml:
3. Manifestation

The Cold War had been a race between the two superpowers — the US and USSR — to spread their ideologies and prevent the enemy from doing so. This conflict spilled over into other parts of the world, and proxy wars broke out in Asia where, much like the Iron Curtain, the Bamboo Curtain had formed between communists and non-communists.

Proxy War: Armed conflict between two states or non-state actors which act on the instigation or on behalf of other parties that are not directly involved in the hostilities.

The Korean War

As the Japanese pulled out of the Korean peninsula, the USSR and USA liberated the nation from the North and South respectively. Conflict arose between the leaders of the Communist North and Capitalist South, developing into a Civil War. The war soon transformed into the first major proxy war of the Cold War, as the USSR and China supported their fellow communist counterpart against the US and UN backed South.

Belligerents

North Korea — Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK); South Korea — Republic of Korea (ROK).

Leaders

  • Kim Il Sung (Premier and Dictator of North Korea): Communist leader trained and backed by the USSR (influenced by and supported policies of purges, collectivisation and industrialisation; installed by Stalin). Ran a Soviet-style one-party system; dictatorship, totalitarianism. Wanted to unify Korea by force and impose communism on the whole peninsula. Used a militaristic style of governance — extending military influence into civilian social, political and economic spheres, prioritising and preserving the armed forces.
  • Syngman Rhee (First President of South Korea): Anti-communist dictator. Wanted to unify Korea under the banner of capitalism. Authoritarian and responsible for many massacres. Mass-arrested political opponents.

Supporters

  • USSR: Wanted to secure the Korean Peninsula and include it in the communist bloc to maintain its growing power. Due to the successes of communism in the region, Stalin had become determined to increase his influence.
  • China: Due to its geographical proximity to Korea, it could act as a platform to spread communism in the Asia-Pacific region, establishing satellite states.
  • USA: Initially, Korea was not a priority for the US. As communism had succeeded in China and the USSR gained atomic power, the US became increasingly alarmed. China had fallen to communism, and Stalin had been encouraging communists in other countries (Malaya and Vietnam) to rise up against their colonial powers. The US saw the threat of an international communist movement and, fearing the establishment of a communist stronghold in the Asia-Pacific, took a harder stance against communist influence. In the 1950s, there was public pressure on the American government to be more proactive in resisting the spread of communism — this resulted in NSC-68, which influenced American foreign policy towards the USSR over the next 20 years.
  • UN: The US believed the UN had to take a firm stand on Korea or risk losing its credibility as an agency protecting international security, thus sponsoring many UNSC resolutions.

Key Figures

  • Joseph Stalin — Dictator and leader of the Soviet Union. Advised Kim throughout the war and fought with the West to spread communism.
  • Mao Zedong — Chairman of the Communist Party of China and leader of China. He was afraid of anti-communists at his doorstep and claimed to be intervening as the US was entering Korea through the guise of the UN. The Soviet Union sent supplies to aid China's effort in Korea.
  • Zhou Enlai — Premier of China. Oversaw the Korean War for China, as he feared anti-communists coming to power in Korea. "Korea is China's neighbor... The Chinese people cannot but be concerned about a solution of the Korean question" — Zhou Enlai, speaking to the United Nations.
  • Douglas MacArthur — Commander-in-chief of UN operations in Korea. Seen as a military genius but tended to ignore commands from higher-ups (Truman). He mistakenly assumed China would not get involved in the war and was accused of wanting to use nuclear weapons in Korea. A showboat and prone to political grandstanding, he was relieved of command during the war.
  • Harry S. Truman — President of the United States. A strong anti-communist concerned with the spread of communism; responsible for bringing the US and UN into the Korean War.

Background

Japan invaded and occupied Korea from 1905–1945, becoming a colony of Imperial Japan. After the defeat of Japan, Korea was freed by the USA from the South and the USSR from the North, meeting and splitting the country at the 38th parallel. By 1949, the USA and USSR had pulled their troops out of Korea (the US removed troops 4 months later), leaving Kim Il Sung and Syngman Rhee to govern the North and South respectively. The North Korean army left behind was well-trained and well-armed compared to the poorly trained and equipped small force that comprised the South Korean army.

In 1950, the US government publicly announced a list of countries it was prepared to defend against the Communists (Defence Perimeter); South Korea was not mentioned. Kim believed he could conquer the South and began seeking support from the USSR and China, persuading Stalin. Only in April did Stalin agree, after: (1) Mao had secured a communist victory in the Chinese Civil War; (2) US troops had withdrawn from South Korea; and (3) the USSR had successfully tested their first nuclear weapons. The USSR and China, after approving the invasion, started sending aid via weapons and advisers to the North.

Superpower Involvement

Northern Support: (1) Military and Economic Aid — From 1948, the USSR had been involved in training and organising the North Korean army. Emboldened by developments in Asia, Stalin also sent Soviet military advisors, tanks, guns, artillery, aircraft, fighter planes and attack bombers to arm the North, creating a formidable force compared to the poorly trained and equipped South, which had received limited support from the US (due to concerns over Rhee's authoritarian government) — causing a power imbalance that allowed a smooth invasion. After UN intervention, 200,000 Chinese troops crossed the border, providing much-needed support for the North Korean army and pushing UN forces back to the 38th parallel. (2) Installation of a Political Figure — Kim had been trained in the USSR and served in the Soviet Army as a Korean guerrilla. After the Japanese left, the USSR installed him as leader in North Korea, placing the region under communist control. Over the course of the war, both Mao and Stalin showed support for Kim's regime.

Southern Support: Military Intervention — After the invasion, a coalition of US and UN troops was sent to resist the North Korean army. UN forces provided strong leadership, organisational skills and war strategies against North Korea, successfully cutting supply and communication lines by outflanking them and driving them back North, giving the South a temporary victory.

Timeline of the Korean War

  • North Korea invaded South Korea, officially starting the Korean War.
  • The UN Security Council unanimously condemned the invasion with UNSC Resolution 82, calling for North Korea to immediately halt its invasion and move its troops back to the 38th parallel. This was totally ignored by North Korea.
  • Two days later, the UNSC adopted Resolution 83, determining the invasion as a breach of peace and once again calling for the terms of Resolution 82, noting it was ignored. It authorised UN member states to provide military assistance to South Korea. (The USSR could have vetoed the resolution, but was boycotting the council meeting as the Republic of China/Taiwan was still occupying China's seat in the UNSC.)
  • On 27 June 1950, the North captured the Southern capital of Seoul, driving Rhee and other leaders further South. The North Korean army continued its advance South.
  • A UN force of 16 member countries entered the war against North Korea, with half the soldiers from the USA.
  • North Korean troops reached their farthest point of advance, controlling almost the entire Korean peninsula apart from the port city of Pusan, which remained under Southern control.
  • On 15 September 1950, UN forces staged an ambitious landing at Incheon, facing very little opposition. One day later, UN and South Korean troops began to break out of the Pusan Perimeter, advancing North and pushing North Korean troops back quickly.
  • Although the retaliation was only meant to stop the invasion, coalition troops crossed the 38th parallel and took over the Northern capital of Pyongyang.
  • In late 1950, as UN troops approached the Chinese border, around 200,000 Chinese People's Volunteers crossed into North Korea to aid Northern troops, dealing a heavy blow to the advancing UN forces.
  • On 11 April 1951, General MacArthur was relieved of command for insubordination. He had crossed the 38th parallel, mistakenly believing China would not intervene, threatened to destroy China unless they surrendered, and believed the use of atomic bombs was necessary. Truman wanted to avoid a third world war with China and the USSR.
  • Chinese troops proved effective in pushing UN troops back to the South. By February 1951, they had forced a stalemate just South of the 38th parallel.
  • In June 1951, negotiations for a peace settlement began. After 2 more years of fighting, an armistice was reached on 27 July 1953, though no actual peace settlement was decided.

From this timeline, there were drastic changes during the course of the Korean War. Hence provenance is very important for SBQ analysis: sources before 12 September 1950 must be considered with the fact that the US and UN had not yet carried out large-scale intervention in Korea, while sources after 25 October 1950 must be considered in light of MacArthur's ambitions.

NSC-68: Rollback

National Security Council Paper NSC-68 was a Top-Secret report completed by the U.S. Department of State's Policy Planning Staff on 7 April 1950. The 58-page memorandum is among the most influential documents composed by the U.S. Government during the Cold War, and was not declassified until 1975. Its authors argued that one of the most pressing threats confronting the United States was the "hostile design" of the Soviet Union, and that this threat would soon be greatly augmented by the addition of more weapons, including nuclear weapons, to the Soviet arsenal. They argued that the best course of action was to respond in kind with a massive build-up of the U.S. military and its weaponry, and to eliminate communism entirely. During the war, the defence budget quadrupled, influencing US policy with the USSR.

Impacts of the War

For Korea:

  • Division of Korea: Though an armistice was signed and fighting soon stopped, no actual peace treaty was signed, as both sides could not agree on how to unite Korea. Both nations remain technically at war, divided by a demilitarised zone at the 38th parallel. Families living on opposite sides could not visit or even communicate with each other.
  • Loss of Lives: In the 3 years of war, Korean civilian casualties — dead, wounded and missing — totalled between 3–4 million.
  • Korean Economy: More than 80% of factories and transport networks were destroyed as a result of the war, effectively destroying most of its economy. North Korea eventually fell into poverty and was unable to keep up with South Korea's development, creating a wealth gap between the two countries.

For the USA:

  • US Foreign Policy: The realisation of an international communist movement led to the 'domino theory' gaining traction. Although the US succeeded in preventing South Korea from falling to communism, the war influenced how they would approach the threat of communism in Asia for the next 20 years.
  • Militarisation of the Region: The war led to massive American rearmament. Their defence budget shot up to $48 billion in 1951 and $60 billion by 1952. The USA also made a series of alliances, including one with the Philippines, and in 1951 signed the ANZUS Pact with Australia and New Zealand.

For USSR/China:

  • China's Reputation: China's power had been greatly underestimated by the Western nations. China proved its prowess through the war, holding out against American forces. Westerners began to treat China more seriously, and it was admitted into the UN in 1971.
  • Sino-Soviet Relations: Arguments between both powers over the bill for the war affected their alliance. The Chinese came to feel the Soviet Union was both an unreliable and demanding ally, and took greater steps to ensure independence from the USSR in the years following the war. In 1960, China broke from the Soviet Union in the Sino-Soviet Split, creating tension amongst communist powers.

International Relations

  • The Korean War seemed to confirm the view of a worldwide communist conspiracy and ensured the Cold War spread to Asia.
  • The war strengthened the determination of the USA to contain communism on a worldwide scale.
  • The war established the pattern whereby if one superpower was directly involved, the other was indirectly associated — the first time the two superpowers fought a proxy war in a third country.
  • The Korean War was an important development in the Cold War because, as a result of the war and General MacArthur's dismissal, the strategy of rollback was largely discredited.
  • The temporary division of Korea along the 38th parallel was a success for the policy of containment, as communism did not spread into South Korea.
  • In 1954, SEATO (South East Asian Treaty Organisation) was set up as a copy of NATO. Communism had been prevented in South Korea, and the UN was seen as a success.
  • However, the war revealed that China was no longer weak and was prepared to stand up to the West. The fear in the West was that China would emerge as a third superpower.
  • The split between China and the USSR was influenced by the Korean War and shaped relations between the two countries until 1989. The USA was keen to make the most of this tension later in the Cold War.

Additional Information

  • As Japanese forces in Korea surrendered at the close of WWII, Soviet troops had already been deployed in North Korea and were approaching the South. The United States swiftly proposed splitting Korea into zones in an attempt to prevent the Soviets from occupying the entire nation.
  • Two American generals were tasked with dividing Korea into two zones and decided to split it across the 38th Parallel (a straight line on the map), which Russia agreed to.
  • Korea had always been one country, so the split across the 38th Parallel was disruptive to Koreans — it cut across railways, roads and neighbourhoods, dividing the Korean people, who had no say in the division. It was planned as a temporary division with the goal of eventually unifying the two Koreas, but with the subsequent falling out of the USA and USSR, it would soon become permanent.
  • The Korean people celebrated the arrival of the USA and USSR and were happy to take on the respective ideologies (capitalism/communism), as they had been treated extremely poorly during Japanese colonisation. There was some element of loyalty and admiration among Koreans for the leaders of the USA and USSR as their 'liberators' from Japanese tyranny.

shortAnswer.prompt: "Korea is China's neighbor... The Chinese people cannot but be concerned about a solution of the Korean question" — Zhou Enlai, speaking to the United Nations. What can you infer about China's motives for intervening in the Korean War from this source?
shortAnswer.modelAnswer: The message of the source is that China framed its intervention in Korea as motivated by genuine security concern over a neighbouring country's fate, rather than pure ideological expansion. This is shown through the phrase 'Korea is China's neighbor' and the claim that 'the Chinese people cannot but be concerned', suggesting China wanted to present its involvement as a natural, almost unavoidable response to a security threat on its border. This aligns with the context that China feared US/UN forces approaching the Yalu River threatened Chinese security, and that Mao believed the US was entering Korea 'through the guise of the UN.'
rubric: Makes a clear inference (framing intervention as security-driven, not just ideological)
Supports the inference with a direct quotation from the source
Explains the link between quotation and inference
Uses contextual knowledge (UN forces near Yalu River, Mao's fear of the US using the UN as a guise)

shortAnswer.prompt: How reliable is Zhou Enlai's statement to the United Nations as evidence of China's true reasons for entering the Korean War?
shortAnswer.modelAnswer: Zhou Enlai's statement is only partly reliable. On one hand, it is supported by contextual knowledge that China genuinely feared a security threat from UN/US forces approaching its border and wished to prevent an anti-communist government emerging in Korea, so the concern expressed is not baseless. However, upon closer examination of the provenance and purpose, Zhou Enlai was speaking as an official representative of China to the United Nations, an international audience, and his likely purpose was to justify China's planned or actual intervention as reasonable and defensive rather than aggressive expansion, meaning the statement may downplay China's own ambitions (e.g. Mao's vision to extend communist influence in Asia) in favour of a more sympathetic framing. Thus, while the underlying security concern is factually supported, the statement's one-sided framing limits its reliability as a full account of China's motives.
rubric: First paragraph: inference with source content and evidence
Second paragraph: cross-reference to contextual knowledge (China's security fears)
Third paragraph: critical analysis of provenance/purpose (Zhou Enlai, UN audience, official justification)
Clear concluding link back to 'reliable' as worded in the question

shortAnswer.prompt: Assess the extent to which the Korean War can be considered a success for the American policy of containment.
shortAnswer.modelAnswer: The Korean War can be considered a partial success for containment: the temporary division of Korea along the 38th parallel meant communism did not spread into South Korea, and the war reinforced US determination to contain communism worldwide, leading to alliances like SEATO and ANZUS. However, it was not a complete triumph, since General MacArthur's rollback strategy (pushing into North Korea) was discredited after his dismissal, and China's entry revealed it was no longer a weak power, raising Western fears it might emerge as a third superpower. Additionally, no formal peace treaty was achieved, leaving an unresolved, costly standoff. Thus while containment succeeded narrowly in preventing South Korea's fall to communism, the war also exposed the limits and costs of pursuing an aggressive rollback beyond containment.
rubric: Directly addresses containment as the given factor with a clear stand
Uses specific evidence (38th parallel division, SEATO, ANZUS) to support success
Weighs against evidence of limitation/failure (rollback discredited, China's rising power, no peace treaty)
Reaches a balanced, reasoned concluding judgement

topics.title: The Vietnam War
topics.notesHtml:
The Vietnam War

Much like Korea, post-WWII Vietnam had been divided into the North and South, communists and capitalists. Vietnam had suffered greatly under the hands of multiple powers, and for many, this was a fight for independence. However, the difference in ideologies and fear of the 'Domino Theory' (that if one country fell to communism, other proximal nations would soon fall too) got the US involved yet again, fighting in the dense jungles of Indochina. The war marked one of the USA's greatest defeats, as many innocent civilians, US soldiers and Viet Cong guerrillas died in both conflicts and massacres.

Background

  • 111 BC – 1427 AD: Chinese Rule and Influence — Since ancient times, Vietnam had been under the influence of China, at times under the rule of various Chinese dynasties. For almost 1000 years, China had tried to absorb Vietnam into itself through both conquest and cultural assimilation. This stopped in the 19th century as China faced its own problems with colonisation and Western imperialism.
  • 1887 – 1945: French Occupation — In the 19th century, the French colonial empire took over the regions of Cambodia, Laos and Vietnam collectively under the union of French Indochina. The Vietnamese state had capitulated and been reduced to a puppet administration with no oversight over the country's affairs. French occupiers exploited the region's natural resources and peasant population for self-benefit. Any sign of nationalistic resistance was dealt with by force, evident by decades of failed rebellions and uprisings. Vietnamese peasants grew desperate to escape their French colonisers.
  • 1940 – 1945: Japanese Invasion — Under its expansionist foreign policy, Imperial Japan set her eyes on French Indochina, wanting to create an 'Asia for Asians' under the Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere, where Western colonists would be driven out of the region. In 1940, Japan annexed Indochina, occupying it for the next 5 years until losing the war in 1945. Under Japanese rule, French colonisers continued Vietnamese administration, instead working for the Japanese (under Vichy France). During the Japanese occupation, a strong anti-Japanese movement (Viet Minh) emerged under the leadership of communist Ho Chi Minh, who inspired the Vietnamese people to resist and fight their Japanese occupiers. In 1945, the Viet Minh entered the northern city of Hanoi and declared Vietnam independent.

Bảo Đại

Final Emperor of the Nguyen Dynasty, the last ruling family of Vietnam. French-educated and spent much of his time outside Vietnam. Installed as a puppet leader by the French and later the Japanese. Cooperated with the French and had pro-French ideals, making him unpopular with the populace. Ousted by Ngô Đình Diệm in 1955.

1945 – 1954: French Return and the Indochina War

In 1946, after the war, French leader Charles De Gaulle was determined to reassert sovereignty over Indochina, which was met with resistance from the Vietminh, who campaigned for Vietnamese independence. What followed was 9 years of bitter war between the Vietminh-controlled North and French-controlled South. Ho was supported by China, which had recently become a communist state in 1949. The US, as seen from the Truman Doctrine, responded by helping those who opposed the communists, pouring $500 million into the French war effort. American aid was to no avail. In 1954, after a decisive Vietminh victory at Dien Bien Phu, the defeated France withdrew all forces from their colonies in French Indochina.

Belligerents

North Vietnam — Democratic Republic of Vietnam (DRV); South Vietnam — Republic of Vietnam.

Leaders

  • Hồ Chí Minh (Prime Minister and President of North Vietnam): Nationalistic and Communist. Fought for Vietnamese independence since French rule. Created the Viet Minh to resist Japanese invaders, led the war against the French return, and later became a symbol for the reunification of Vietnam. Served as Vietnam's head of state and main point of contact between the Vietnamese and foreign powers (US, France). Advocated peace but was dragged into the war by his more militant followers. Refused negotiations due to the intense bombing by the Americans. Had massive civilian support.
  • Ngô Đình Diệm (First President of South Vietnam, assassinated): Dictator supported by the US. Belonged to the landlord class; treated peasants with contempt. Did not respect democracy; ruled by nepotism. Showed preference for Catholics; his government persecuted Buddhists, leading to opposition from the Viet Minh, Buddhists and intellectuals. Economic aid was diverted to corruption. Removed during a military coup supported by the CIA in 1963.

Supporters

  • Leonid Brezhnev (Dictator and leader of the Soviet Union): Supported the North Vietnamese guerrillas fighting against the Americans with military advisors and financial aid. This helped prevent loss of Soviet influence in Southeast Asia and bolster its position as the authority in communist movements.
  • Mao Zedong (Chairman of the Communist Party of China): Had a vision to be leader of international revolutionary communism and was keen to extend communist influence to Southeast Asia. Also feared American intervention in Vietnam would lead to a security threat towards China, and provided economic and military support to North Vietnam.
  • USA: Presidents Roosevelt, Truman (involved in the First Indochina War), Eisenhower, Kennedy, Johnson and Nixon. Over the course of the war, the US president changed constantly, clearly reflected by the changing US stance in Vietnam, shifting from support, to concern, to aggression, and to resignation.

Key Events

1954 Geneva Conference: As per the 1954 Geneva Accords, Indochina would be free from French control and partitioned into three successor states: the Kingdom of Cambodia, the Kingdom of Laos, and Vietnam, which was split into the North and South at the 17th parallel until 1956, when democratic elections could be held to decide its future. All parties agreed to the terms except the US, who believed in the Domino Theory. Ho Chi Minh had much support from the Vietnamese population, and the US was convinced he would win the election, making Vietnam a communist state. Diem later refused to hold the unification elections, leaving Vietnam divided into two states.

Gulf of Tonkin Incident (2 August 1964): North Vietnamese patrol boats in the Gulf of Tonkin attacked the USS Maddox and USS Turner Joy. This attack, later known as the Gulf of Tonkin Incident, paved the way for the US to respond with direct military intervention. The US Congress, angered by the attack, passed the Tonkin Gulf Resolution, authorising President Lyndon Johnson to "take all necessary measures to repel any armed attack against the forces of the United States and to prevent further aggression". The resolution effectively launched America's full-scale involvement in the Vietnam War, sending troops instead of advisors to fight in Vietnam.

Tet Offensive (31 January 1968): A coordinated series of North Vietnamese attacks on more than 100 cities and outposts in South Vietnam. One Viet Cong unit tried to capture the US embassy in Saigon. The offensive was an attempt to foment rebellion among the South Vietnamese population and to encourage the United States to scale back its involvement in the war. The communists suffered heavily, failing to start an uprising in the South and losing many experienced soldiers. Though US and South Vietnamese forces managed to hold off the attacks, news coverage of the massive offensive shocked the American public and eroded support for the war effort. The attacks marked a turning point in the war and the beginning of the slow, painful American withdrawal from the region.

War Tactics

Unlike Korea, Vietnam was a tropical country with many rainforests and mountains. Due to this unique geography, both sides adopted new methods of warfare.

  • Guerrilla Warfare (Viet Cong): Given that the Viet Cong had much less manpower and inferior firepower, a direct clash with the southern forces would guarantee a loss. Therefore, the Viet Cong employed guerrilla warfare, where small groups of soldiers disguised in civilian clothing would ambush the enemy, destroying their supplies and morale.
  • Ho Chi Minh Trail: Used as a route for the North to supply Viet Cong soldiers in the South. The trail passed through Laos and Cambodia, allowing the more resource-abundant North to bail out the southern resistance fighters. As a result, the route was subject to frequent bombing, although the Vietnamese still worked hard to keep supplies moving through it.
  • Cu Chi Tunnels: A series of tunnel and cave complexes underground, providing the Viet Cong with a spot to hide and reside in. The vast tunnels contained wells, sleeping areas, and even hospitals and kitchens. Booby traps were employed to injure enemies who wandered into the caves. The US trained dedicated 'tunnel rats' to search and scout these tunnels.
  • Napalm, Agent Orange and Explosives (Southern/US troops): Such defoliating agents removed bushes and other vegetation, removing hiding spots for the Viet Cong.
  • Bombing: North and South Vietnam were bombed by US bombers. In 1965, a series of bombings of North Vietnam commenced after the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution, known as Operation Rolling Thunder. Bombings of South Vietnam, however, were not effective, as Viet Cong troops often took cover in the Cu Chi tunnels, safely sheltered from the bombs. Vietnamese civilians and peasants, however, were adversely affected by the bombings, as many were injured and farmland and crops were destroyed. They had to live in fear, and this largely turned Vietnamese support against the Americans.

US Involvement in Vietnam

ReasonElaboration
Containment PolicyThe US thought the USSR was directing the Communist movement in Vietnam. This caused great concern, as the US did not want communism to spread any further, demanding action.
IdeologySouth Vietnam had similar ideologies to the US, being democratic and capitalist. The US felt an obligation to support South Vietnam and saw it as an opportunity to spread its influence in Asia.
EconomicsA communist Vietnam would certainly close its doors to American trade, affecting the US economy. Intervention was needed, in the eyes of the US, to maintain an open door to US trade in Vietnam.
SecurityAsia already had China, the communist world superpower. The rest of Asia should be kept non-communist in order to balance power in the region.
US PoliticsUS politicians had to appear strong in the fight against the spread of communism in order to win support from an American public deeply afraid of communism. With elections at stake, politicians moved to prove through actions that they were against the spread of communism.
Domino TheoryThe US feared that if Vietnam fell to communism, the ideology would spread further, causing Thailand, Bangladesh, India, Malaysia, Singapore and later the whole region to fall under communist rule. They felt it necessary to stop it at the very start before it was too late.

Anti-War Campaigns in America

Anti-Vietnam War campaigns were mostly spurred by the Tet Offensive, where Americans realised the Vietnam War was not going to end soon and that there was still a long struggle ahead. In 1967, a large-scale protest known as the March on the Pentagon was held to bring an end to the war.

ReasonExplanation
No room for victoryThe Tet Offensive showed that the North Vietnamese were capable of launching large-scale attacks on South Vietnam. This shook confidence in US public opinion regarding America's ability to win the Vietnam War. When General Westmoreland requested more than 200,000 new troops to mount an effective counteroffensive, many Americans saw it as an act of desperation.
Heavy costs of lives and moneyEven before the Tet Offensive, by November 1967, American troop strength in Vietnam was approaching 500,000, and US casualties had reached 15,058 killed and 109,527 wounded. The Vietnam War was costing the US some $25 billion per year, and disillusionment was beginning to reach greater sections of the taxpaying public. More casualties were reported in Vietnam every day, and US commanders demanded more troops. Under the draft system, as many as 40,000 young men were called into service each month, adding fuel to the anti-war movement.
Horrific atrocities committed by American soldiersWar crimes committed by the Americans also shocked the US, after incidents like the My Lai Massacre were discovered. The media covered events of the war extensively, showing images of injured, crying children, houses on fire and tortured prisoners, causing many in the US to question the purpose of the war.
InequalityConscription of American troops to fight in Vietnam exposed racial inequality in the US.

Note: the source material is truncated at this point in the notes.

shortAnswer.prompt: Compare US involvement in the Korean War and the Vietnam War in terms of the reasons behind American intervention. How similar were the two?
shortAnswer.modelAnswer: US involvement in Korea and Vietnam is similar in that both interventions were driven by the containment policy and fear of the Domino Theory: in Korea, the US feared a communist takeover of the peninsula following China's fall to communism, while in Vietnam, the US feared that a communist Vietnam would trigger the fall of Thailand, Malaysia, and other neighbouring states. Both cases also involved US concern for maintaining credibility (via the UN in Korea, and through US politics/elections in Vietnam) and protecting economic interests (open markets for trade). However, the two differ in the nature of the fighting: Korea involved more conventional warfare with UN-sanctioned troop deployments, while Vietnam involved guerrilla warfare and a much larger, more controversial and prolonged US troop commitment that ultimately generated strong domestic anti-war opposition, which was less pronounced in Korea.
rubric: Uses the correct comparative word ('similar') as per the question
Provides specific evidence from both wars (containment, domino theory, credibility)

Concludes with an overarching judgement on the comparison

shortAnswer.prompt: Assess the extent to which the Tet Offensive (1968) was the primary turning point that led to US withdrawal from Vietnam.
shortAnswer.modelAnswer: The Tet Offensive was a very significant turning point: although communist forces suffered heavy losses and failed to spark an uprising, the shock of over 100 South Vietnamese cities being attacked, combined with extensive news coverage, eroded American public confidence that the war could be won, especially after General Westmoreland's request for 200,000 more troops was seen as desperation. This directly triggered growing anti-war sentiment and the beginning of the slow American withdrawal. However, it was not the sole cause: mounting casualties and financial costs (US troop strength approaching 500,000 and costs of $25 billion per year by late 1967) and revelations of atrocities like the My Lai Massacre also fuelled disillusionment, meaning Tet accelerated and crystallised existing discontent rather than being the sole trigger. Thus, Tet was the key catalytic turning point, but it worked alongside pre-existing costs and moral concerns to drive US withdrawal.

Uses specific evidence (Westmoreland's troop request, casualty/cost figures, My Lai)

topics.title: End of the Vietnam War and Impacts
topics.notesHtml:
End of the War and Impacts

America's Withdrawal from Vietnam

By 1973, US Secretary of State Henry Kissinger had secured a peace agreement with North Vietnam. Under the agreement, the US had to withdraw all of its troops within 60 days. The South Vietnamese were left alone, although economic aid was still supplied by the US. Without US support, the South eventually fell to the North.

Paris Peace Accords

At the end of the war, President Johnson eventually lost support from the American people for his poor role and management of the Vietnam War, and was succeeded by President Richard Nixon, who worked towards ending American involvement in Vietnam together with Henry Kissinger. However, no concrete progress was made towards peace until the Paris Peace Accords of January 1973 (both North and South Vietnam had earlier refused to sign agreements proposed by the US-UN).

Eventually, the Paris Peace Accords led to the signing of a mutual agreement that ended the war and restored peace among the USA, North Vietnam and South Vietnam.

Reunification and Independence of Vietnam

  • North Vietnam refused to hold elections
  • South Vietnam could not hold on to power without US help
  • North Vietnam invaded South Vietnam
  • 1975: North and South Vietnam unified under communism, with the capture of Saigon

topics.title: Cuban Missile Crisis: Background and Cuban Revolution
topics.notesHtml:
Cuban Missile Crisis

The Cuban Missile Crisis (CMC) is a key instance of brinkmanship — the practice of trying to achieve an advantageous outcome by pushing dangerous events to the brink of active conflict. The CMC marks a critical point in the Cold War, being the first time the United States was directly threatened by nuclear destruction. The Cuban Missile Crisis lasted 13 days, from 16th to 28th October 1962.

Background: Why was Cuba significant to the US?

AspectWhat was Cuba?Why did it matter to the US?
EconomicCuba was a Spanish colony and centre of commerce in the Americas region. It was a major producer of rum, sugar and tobacco, which were in high demand in both Europe and America.Taking Cuba would mean the US could use the island for American business interests, taking advantage of the island's products and benefitting its trade and economy.
GeopoliticalCuba was in close proximity to the US, located between the US and the Caribbean islands.The US saw the Americas as its own sphere of influence, and Cuba was its gateway to extending power over the Caribbean. The island would be strategic in the US plan to expand its power and ensure its security.

Early American Involvement in Cuba

In 1898, Cuba struggled to fight against the Spanish in the Cuban War of Independence. The US intervened, supporting the Cuban independence fighters, and America won the war. Even after withdrawing troops from Cuba in 1902, the US continued its interests in the region.

Political:

  • Although the US promised to hand over power to an independent and democratic Cuban government, it had established a pro-US government friendly to American political and economic interests.
  • The Cuban government was not allowed to make alliances with other nations without US approval.
  • America frequently intervened in Cuban politics to maintain US security, installing "puppet presidents" to guard national interests, much to the resentment of Cuban nationalists.

Fulgencio Batista — the final "puppet president" of Cuba:

  • Corrupt and dictatorial, oppressing the Cuban people and violently persecuting opponents.
  • Had ties with the mafia, allowing them to control illegal business in Havana and big US corporations in Cuba.
  • Used secret police to remove opponents.
  • The US was nonetheless reluctant to withdraw support, for fear of communism being brought by his opponents into their backyard.

Economic:

  • Due to the pro-US government, US companies invested heavily in Cuba and in improving its infrastructure.
  • In 1962, the US owned 60% of the Cuban sugar industry and was a major market for its sugar and tobacco produce.
  • Many Cubans resented US economic dominance, which made Cuba vulnerable to sudden and drastic changes in the price of sugar, and created a large income gap between a small group of rich Cuban elites who worked with US investors and the majority of poor Cubans (inequality).

Key Terms and Recap

  • Cuban Missile Crisis — a key instance of brinkmanship, the practice of trying to achieve an advantageous outcome by pushing dangerous events to the brink of active conflict.
  • Havana — a centre of commerce in the 19th century and a major producer of sugar and tobacco, in high demand in Europe and the USA, making it of great importance to any power wanting to control the region.
  • The US essentially installed a puppet government in Cuba (Batista — corrupt, dictatorial, with ties to the mafia that allowed it to control illegal businesses in Havana and massive US corporations in Cuba; secret police used violence to remove opponents, but the US was reluctant to withdraw support for Batista as it may have meant Cuba falling to communism).
  • Resentment towards the US grew for creating an elite class of Cubans (those who supported them) while the unsupportive majority lived in poverty.

Cuban Revolution

Fidel Castro was initially a nationalist, not a communist, but due to his disillusionment with the USA, he decided to pledge allegiance to USSR-style communism, seeing similarities between his ideals and the USSR's, and began to develop Marxist policies.

Act/ActionCuba's RationaleUS Response
Seeking new markets for Cuban sugar: Cuba's Minister of Industries, Che Guevara, visited various countries in 1959 to seek new markets for Cuban sugar.Cuba's economy was heavily reliant on the American Sugar Quota, which determined the amount and price of sugar the USA bought from Cuba. This subjected Cuba's economy to American influence and made it vulnerable to America's economic fluctuations. Hence, Cuba had to reduce its reliance on the USA for the sale of its sugar.Sanctions
Land Reform Law: The agrarian reforms in Cuba sought to break up large landholdings and redistribute land to the peasants who worked it, to cooperatives, and to the state.To fulfil Castro's promise to the peasants who supported him during the Cuban Revolution. 
Castro's friendship with Khrushchev.Allowed the USSR to use Cuba as leverage (to place their missiles) and therefore as a means to threaten the USA. 
  • This was an instance of the Americans being unable to simply let Cuba be, interfering in foreign affairs (e.g. Operation Mongoose) — a common thread in US foreign policy in the post-WWII era (e.g. also seen with Saddam Hussein, Osama bin Laden).
  • Cuba aligned itself with the USSR because the USSR was the major antagonist of the USA, and the corruption of the US-instituted government in Cuba and its constant meddling in Cuban affairs angered many Americans. This drove Cuba towards the USSR as a form of protection and defense against the USA.
  • Castro pledged himself to be a Marxist-Leninist, establishing a communist party in Cuba.

Other Events at the Time

  • Construction of the Berlin Wall — divided East and West Germany; those who tried to mount the wall and leave East Germany were shot/killed.
  • Sino-Soviet Split — Khrushchev began a process of 'de-Stalinization' which angered Mao, a Stalin sympathiser. He denounced the Soviet leadership as revisionist.

Reasons for Soviet Installation of Missiles

  • Strategically, it was a response to the USA's installation of missiles in Turkey, an "eye-for-an-eye" move that ensured the USSR had its own protection against potential American nuclear threats.
  • Politically, it allowed the USSR leverage over the USA, enabling it to make demands/force concessions using the tangible threat of nuclear attack.
  • Castro reluctantly agreed to the placement of the missiles, knowing it would heighten the risk of nuclear war, but still wanting to protect Cuba's national interests.

topics.title: Cuban Missile Crisis: Timeline
topics.notesHtml:
Cuban Missile Crisis Timeline

  1. 16th October — After US spy planes discover medium-range ballistic missiles in Cuba, and that the missile bases were for offensive weaponry, Kennedy is informed of the threat and gathers a group of advisors (later known as the Executive Committee/National Security Council) to consider potential measures to diffuse the situation.
  2. 17th October — Kennedy spends the day meeting with advisors, discussing various courses of action and their potential consequences, and realises the grave possibility of war.
  3. 18th October — The Soviet Union lies to Kennedy, claiming the missile sites were only for defensive purposes, not offensive reasons. This leads Kennedy to order further spy jets over Cuba, which discover seven more missile sites, including medium and long-range missiles (the excessive number of sites and the range of the missiles signalled to the US that they were for offensive purposes).
  4. 19th October — The escalating threat leads Kennedy to cancel a campaign stop in Chicago so he can return to Washington. The media is told the President must return due to a "cold"; the real reasons are withheld.
  5. 20th October — The US begins to make military preparations as it determines its course of action moving forward, teetering on the strategy of brinkmanship.
  6. 21st October — The US notifies its allies of the growing threat in Cuba and the escalating tensions with the USSR.
  7. 22nd October — President Kennedy goes live on national television to inform US citizens of the looming danger of nuclear war.
  8. 23rd October — Kennedy orders a naval blockade of Cuba, intended to prevent weapons and military equipment from reaching the country.
  9. 24th October — At 10am EDT, the blockade goes into effect. It is dubbed a "quarantine", as a blockade is perceived as an act of war under International Law; a 'quarantine' limited the restriction to offensive weapons, which would be more reasonable to the rest of the world, implying the US was not trying to deny Cuba weapons for self-defense or trying to starve the Cuban people. The USSR was shocked and outraged, condemning the blockade as an illegal act of war against Cuba. Khrushchev wrote to Castro assuring continued USSR support and that they would ignore the blockade, but simultaneously ordered recently-departed Soviet ships to return to port to prevent further escalation, while urging ships already en route to Cuba to reach their destination faster. Cuba was put on high alert, mobilising more than 300,000 Cuban soldiers, with Castro making a public declaration of his willingness to die fighting. However, Cuba was instructed not to use the missiles by Soviet Defence Minister Malinovsky.
