topics.title: Comparing the Korean War, Vietnam War and Cuban Missile Crisis
topics.notesHtml:
Korean War, Vietnam War and Cuban Missile Crisis Compared

AspectVietnam WarKorean WarCuban Missile Crisis
Cause(s)Caused by the power vacuum created after World War II when Japan surrendered. The Viet Minh, led by Ho Chi Minh, saw an opportunity to rise and set up the Democratic Republic of Vietnam (DRV) with Hanoi as its capital. In 1949, the French-backed Bao Dai set up the State of Vietnam with Saigon as its capital. The conflict (First Indochina War) stretched on for several years before it evolved into a proxy war in 1954. Key factors: superpower involvement (Gulf of Tonkin); difference in ideology (Ho Chi Minh vs Diem); protection of allies/geopolitical significance (Domino Theory).Caused by the power vacuum created after World War II when Japan surrendered. Korea was split in two along the 38th parallel after Japan surrendered its colonies. The conflict was caused by two dictators, Syngman Rhee and Kim Il Sung, both wanting to reunite the Korean peninsula under their respective regimes. This evolved into a proxy war after American and Soviet powers provided support for their respective sides. Key factors: superpower involvement (installation of Kim, training of North Korea, cooperation with UN); difference in ideology (Kim vs Rhee); protection of allies/geopolitical significance (Japan, greater Pacific).Caused by the US instituting a puppet pro-US government in Cuba in the form of Batista, who was corrupt, dictatorial, with ties to the mafia. In 1959, Fidel Castro and a group of rebels, with the backing of the Cuban people, overthrew the government in the Cuban Revolution. Cuba then aligned itself with the USSR, leading to the USSR placing ICBMs in Cuba and the thirteen days of crisis. Key factors: superpower involvement (USSR missiles, Bay of Pigs); difference in ideology (Castro vs US); geopolitical significance (Caribbean, US backyard, resources and economic interests).
Parties InvolvedDemocratic Republic of Vietnam, State of VietnamDemocratic Republic of Korea, Republic of KoreaCommunist Party of Cuba, USA, USSR
Key Political LeadersHo Chi Minh, Bao Dai, Lyndon B. Johnson, Richard NixonKim Il Sung, Syngman Rhee, Harry S. Truman, Joseph StalinFidel Castro, Nikita Khrushchev, John F. Kennedy
Progression of the CrisisThe war started as a proxy war, with the Democratic Republic of Vietnam supported by the Soviet Union (shared communist stance) and the State of Vietnam supported by the United States (capitalism).The war progressed from a civil war into a proxy war, out of fear of the "bamboo curtain" falling on the Korean peninsula. Rhee had the support of the United States and UN troops, while Kim had the support of China and the Soviet Union.The crisis progressed from the antagonistic relationship between the USA and USSR, coupled with rising tensions between Cuba and the USA over Cuba's corrupt, dictatorial puppet government.
Outcome of the CrisisIn January 1973, the United States and North Vietnam concluded a final peace agreement, ending open hostilities between the two nations. However, war between North and South Vietnam continued until 30 April 1975, when DRV forces captured Saigon, renaming it Ho Chi Minh City. Before the fall of Saigon, Operation Frequent Wind, the largest helicopter evacuation in history, was conducted to evacuate over 7,000 American citizens and 'at-risk' Vietnamese from Saigon; the evacuation ended on the morning of 30 April, just as Saigon fell. On 2 July 1976, North and South Vietnam were merged to form the Socialist Republic of Vietnam, as it remains today.The war ended with the Republic of Korea and the Democratic Republic of Korea signing an armistice, ensuring a stalemate between the two Koreas. The progression of peace between the two Koreas only began in January 2018 and is still ongoing to this day.The crisis ended without an actual outbreak of war; after thirteen days of heightened tensions, the USSR agreed to withdraw its missiles from Cuba on condition that the USA did the same in Turkey.
Effects of the CrisisAfter years of warfare, an estimated 2 million Vietnamese were killed, another 3 million wounded, and 12 million more became refugees. Warfare demolished the country's infrastructure and economy, and recovery was slow; under a broad free market policy introduced in 1986, the economy began to improve, boosted by oil export revenues and an influx of foreign capital. Trade and diplomatic relations between Vietnam and the US resumed in the 1990s. In the United States, the effects of the war lingered long after the last troops returned home in 1973 — the nation spent more than $120 billion on the conflict from 1965-73, and this massive spending led to widespread inflation, exacerbated by a worldwide oil crisis in 1973 and skyrocketing fuel prices. The war also pierced the myth of American invincibility and bitterly divided the nation (anti-war/pro-war). Other effects: unification of Vietnam; removal of US troops; loss of lives; contained spread of communism (domino theory proved wrong); shift in US foreign policy towards Rollback; marked China's rise to power.After the war, North and South Korea remained divided. Families were broken up by the war and lived on opposite sides of the demilitarised zone, unable to visit or even communicate with each other. The impact on the civilian population was especially dramatic — Korean civilian casualties (dead, wounded and missing) totalled between three and four million during the three years of war (1950-1953). The war was disastrous for all of Korea, destroying most of its industry, which caused North Korea to fall into poverty and fail to keep up with South Korea's economic pace. topics.title: The United Nations
topics.notesHtml:
The United Nations

The origins of the United Nations lie in the Second World War. During the war, 26 nations forged a coalition to fight the Axis powers. They agreed not to enter into any separate deals with Nazi Germany and its allies, and adopted a set of principles to underpin their efforts: freedom, human rights and justice for all. The UN embodies these principles and represents the culmination of the Allies' efforts.

Founded in 1945, in the aftermath of the war and the horrors of the Holocaust, it was hoped that the UN would be able to prevent such catastrophes from happening in the future by stabilising international relations and giving peace a more secure foundation. The UN is also widely seen as a successor to the failed League of Nations. It is yet another organisation which strives to seek international peace through cooperation with nations and resolving issues through peaceful means.

Main Purposes of the UN

  1. To maintain International Peace and Security
  2. To promote Economic and Social Development
  3. To promote Human Rights

topics.title: End of the Cold War: Detente and External (Foreign) Factors
topics.notesHtml:
End of the Cold War

Background

In the late 1960s to mid-1970s, the Cold War entered a phase of Détente (French: "relaxation"), where both the US and USSR practised a policy of relaxing tensions and coexistence, rather than containment and confrontation. Pioneered by US National Security Adviser Henry Kissinger, alongside Nixon and Brezhnev, it helped manage Cold War competition without Mutually Assured Destruction (MAD) and nuclear escalation, ensuring a brief peace and stability.

Reasons for the Shift to Detente

  • US: Focus on ending the Vietnam War
  • USSR: Achieved Nuclear Parity
  • Both: Avoid MAD

Richard Nixon (POTUS)

  • Visited Beijing in 1972, beginning the normalisation of relations with the PRC after 25 years of diplomatic isolation.
  • First President to visit the USSR.
  • Signed the Strategic Arms Limitation Talks (SALT) and the Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty with Brezhnev.

In 1979 (referenced in the notes as 1974), the USSR invaded Afghanistan, starting the proxy Soviet-Afghan War, which stopped all talk of detente.

External (Foreign) Factors Leading to the End of the Cold War

1. Military Buildup

When Reagan took office as American president, he increased military spending and massively built up the US Armed Forces, knowing that the USSR's weak economy would not be able to catch up. This re-escalated the Cold War, shifting back from the policy of Detente to Rollback.

Strategic Defence Initiative (SDI) [aka 'Star Wars Program']: Announced by Reagan in 1983, the SDI was a missile defence system that intercepted or destroyed any nuclear missiles fired at the US, protecting it from MAD. These measures made the US seem invulnerable to Soviet nuclear missiles, alarming the USSR, which did not have enough money to sustain an arms race.

Pershing II Missiles: In 1983, the US announced that Pershing II missiles would be deployed in West Germany by NATO. These new missiles were mobile, more accurate, and within striking range of the western part of the USSR. This further exacerbated tensions and the arms race.

Able Archer 83 Incident: A military exercise conducted by NATO members around Western Europe and the US was so realistic that the USSR thought it was a ruse for war and a first nuclear strike on the Soviets. In response, the USSR readied its nuclear forces and prepared for war — the second time a nuclear war was narrowly avoided. The incident made Reagan realise that aggression only made MAD more possible and that the Soviets, too, wanted peace. In the following years, he became more willing to work with the USSR on nuclear disarmament.

2. US Economy

Spurred by the oil crisis, Reagan introduced economic policies of economic liberalisation, individual enterprise and reduced reliance on the federal government. This reduced inflation and spurred economic growth in America. The economies of Western Europe had also recovered and started to boom following aid from the Marshall Plan. This allowed the US to have a stable domestic economy and an excess budget for the arms race. The US also used its economic power to pressure the USSR by:

  • Preventing the sale of computers and other technologies to the USSR
  • Signing an agreement with Saudi Arabia to keep the price of oil low
  • Since the USSR was earning hard currency from oil sales, pressuring European allies to stop or delay construction of the pipeline from Europe to the USSR, preventing the USSR from earning hard currency from oil sales

3. Soviet-Afghan War

The Soviet-Afghan War was a 9-year conflict fought between 1979-1989. When the ineffective, Soviet-supported Afghan President was assassinated and anti-government religious fighters gained favour with the population, Brezhnev deployed troops to invade Afghanistan, staging a coup and installing a leader loyal to the USSR. Although a short operation was expected, the conflict soon became a bloody, protracted war with heavy military, economic and diplomatic costs for the USSR. USSR troops struggled in the cold Afghan terrain and met strong resistance from guerrillas supported by Western nations.

topics.title: Internal (Domestic) Factors Behind the USSR's Collapse
topics.notesHtml:
Internal (Domestic) Factors in the Collapse of the USSR

Socioeconomic: Inefficient Economy — Poor Economic Systems

By the late 1970s-80s, the USSR's command economy began to show its inefficiency.

  1. Excessive Military Spending: Years of Cold War and the arms race led to heavy spending on the military; in some years the military took up 50 per cent of government expenditure. As a result, there was little left to produce consumer goods, creating a shortage.
  2. Lack of Consumer Goods: The emphasis on heavy industry and the military meant little attention was paid to consumer goods; quality of life in the USSR was much worse than in capitalist countries.

No Quality Control: The central government focused on targets that were easy to measure. Factory managers waited for instructions on what to produce and at what price. Targets were set only for quantity, not quality, so goods produced were often poor in quality, and many customers were unhappy with the quality of Soviet goods.

Farms and Factories not improved: The central government had not improved farms with technology; factories still used obsolete methods and machines for production. Thus the USSR could not catch up with the West in terms of production.

Inefficient Transport/Distribution System: The USSR's transport and distribution infrastructure was not organised efficiently, partly due to the vastness of the USSR — factories were located far from the raw materials they needed. Due to inefficient transport, much of the crops produced were wasted due to long waiting times.

Inefficient Workers and Social Issues

Alcoholism: A major problem in the USSR, caused partly by the relatively cheap price of alcohol and the lack of other consumer goods for workers to spend on. It created health-related and social problems, which had a bad effect on workforce productivity.

No Working Incentive: In a communist society everyone worked for the state, so there was no reward or incentive to work hard since all were given the same benefits. All Soviet workers were guaranteed jobs for life, so Soviet workers became less efficient than their capitalist counterparts.

Basic needs not met: The command economy could not provide the people with basic necessities. With increased demand for consumer goods, a 'black market' developed, which also meant the government lost a great deal of revenue.

As a result, the USSR was bankrupt — the state had a 35 billion rouble annual deficit, and the military took 50% of the state budget.

Political Factors

Poor and Slow Government Decisions: There were 24,000 loss-making state companies. The central government usually was not aware of local conditions and the problems of the people; due to the size of the USSR, local conditions varied greatly by region, making it hard for the central government to make decisions suitable for all parts of the country. Factory managers often had to wait a long time for decisions to be made by the central government on production, so goods took even longer to reach the shops — this created discontentment among people who found the government ineffective. Agricultural productivity was low, and millions of tons of grain had to be imported.

Conservatism and Corruption: Selection of leaders for the politburo was not based on merit but on favouritism, friendship or seniority, leading to corruption and conservatism. Government officials who controlled goods in short supply often became corrupt, selling goods only to those who could offer a high price.

Unwillingness to Change: The central government/politburo consisted of many leaders unwilling to introduce changes, seeing changes as threats to their positions, so efforts to improve the country were opposed. Most people felt they could not do anything to improve the system and chose not to be involved in politics, so the government was unable to obtain feedback on its performance.

Increased Government Spending: As leader of the Warsaw Pact, the USSR had to spend millions on troops to support its allies. The Soviet Union also gave US$3 billion in subsidies for oil, gas and metals sold to allies, and spent money sponsoring 3rd world communist governments like Cuba. The USSR also provided financial support to Eastern European countries through COMECON. Defence spending increased further when the USSR invaded Afghanistan in 1979. All of this contributed heavily to the USSR's debt.

topics.title: Mikhail Gorbachev: Glasnost, Perestroika and New Thinking
topics.notesHtml:
Mikhail Gorbachev

Gorbachev was the last leader of the Soviet Union (1985-1991). Unlike previous Soviet leaders, although he believed in preserving the Soviet state and socialist ideals, Gorbachev knew that reforms were necessary. He also relied less on fear and oppression to rule the people, instead welcoming the voices of the people on how they should be governed.

His role in the collapse of the USSR remains controversial both internationally and domestically. Though he was the recipient of many awards, including the Nobel Peace Prize, within Russia he is blamed for not stopping the fall of the USSR.

Gorbachev's Policies

When Gorbachev took office, he had 2 objectives:

  1. Restore the people's faith in the communist system of government and end corruption (Glasnost)
  2. Reform Soviet industry and agriculture by adopting elements of the free market system and moving away from central control (Perestroika)

Glasnost ("Openness")

Aim: End corruption and restore people's faith in the communist government.

  1. Make the Soviet government more open and forthcoming in its communication, which had long been restricted:
    • Allowed public freedom of expression and sought to rid public information of propaganda and lies
    • Consulted people about policies instead of just imposing them
    • Allowed media to discuss problems of the nation, including the basic poverty of the Soviet people, waste of the country's resources, and the Chernobyl Disaster

The Chernobyl Disaster (April 1986), where a reactor explosion resulted in the release of radioactive material around the region, was the first instance of Glasnost. Despite obvious health risks, little information was released to the public in the fallout zone, and some reporting was deliberately misleading. Shocked by this response, Gorbachev appeared on Soviet television and gave a speech with a serious admission of the facts of the accident.

  1. Encourage open debate and freedom of speech:
    • Intellectuals, academics, writers and artists who had once criticised the state and were arrested or exiled were released — e.g. Andrei Sakharov, one of the most prominent critics of the communist regime, was allowed back into Moscow after being exiled
    • More forms of media were allowed: banned Soviet fiction from the 1920s-30s was published, and Soviet citizens gained access to Western media outlets like the BBC
    • History of the USSR was uncovered: a good deal of archival material on the Stalinist purges and the Great Terror was unearthed and published; in 1989, Soviet responsibility was finally acknowledged for the Katyn mass murders of Polish soldiers in 1939

Effects: Gorbachev wanted to encourage people to debate freely in order to improve the communist system, not to end it. Instead, people began to call for the end of communist rule. Though the changes under Glasnost were good in that they gave people freedom from decades of political oppression, too much freedom given in such a short span of time meant the danger of confusion amidst liberation — the newfound liberty grew too much for the government to handle. Bitterness and resentment towards the government, built up over 50 years of repression and terror under dictators, surfaced once press censorship ended: people learnt of the government's failures, including corruption, the Afghan-Soviet War, Chernobyl and widespread ecological damage. They began to fiercely criticise Gorbachev and his policies for not improving the situation, and demanded an end to the communist system.

Perestroika ("Reform")

Aim: Reform the Soviet economy (agriculture and industry) by adopting elements of the free market, restructuring the command economy into a demand economy.

  • Ending state monopolies and control of goods; privatisation of state enterprises:
    • 1988 Law on Enterprise: allowed market forces to determine the type and price of goods and workers' wages, and allowed factory managers to manage their own profits, fostering private initiative
    • Legalisation of independent cooperative shops, giving owners control of prices
  • Allowing foreign investment in the USSR through joint ventures with ministries and enterprises

Effects: Gorbachev expected the Soviet economy to be invigorated by increasing the free flow of goods and information, reviving individual initiative and raising living standards. However, Perestroika resulted in numerous negative economic impacts, as the transition to a market economy was too complex for ready and easy solutions:

  • Production and distribution of consumer goods collapsed
  • The economy shrank by 4% in 1990 instead of improving
  • Removal of state controls caused inflation, which rose to 10% in 1989, meaning basic necessities were still unaffordable for ordinary citizens
  • Workers lost their jobs as state-owned companies retrenched staff to reduce costs
  • Factories switched to producing expensive goods rather than basic goods to maximise profits
  • Local governments hoarded essential commodities
  • The black market flourished, as did the Russian Mafia
  • Introduction of private enterprises gave rise to corruption
  • Lines to buy food got longer and fewer basic goods were available

Perestroika had failed terribly, causing the Soviet economy to go from bad to worse and dip below the levels of its previously fledgling command economy. People organised protests against the government to demand more food supplies, while unemployed workers demonstrated in the streets and prevented business from being conducted.

Political Reform and 'New Thinking'

Aim:

  1. Allow Soviet citizens to become more involved at the grassroots level and participate in national affairs, consulting the people about policies instead of just imposing them:
    • The KGB's powers were restricted and corrupt officials were put on trial
    • Gorbachev removed most of the old leaders from power, replacing them with younger leaders more receptive to new ideas
    • Religious freedoms were restored
    • The CPSU held its first conference in 50 years in 1988, and a Congress of People's Deputies was formed, along with a Supreme Soviet
    • March 1989: the first openly contested elections since 1917 were held
  2. Change in Foreign Policy (New Thinking):
    • Reduction in military and defence: the USSR signed an agreement to withdraw from Afghanistan, a process completed by February 1989; defence spending was cut; the "Sinatra Doctrine" ended Soviet military presence in Eastern Europe and around the world
    • Improved relations: 1985 — Gorbachev and Reagan met to discuss nuclear disarmament; 1987 — the INF (Intermediate-Range Nuclear) Treaty was signed with Reagan; 1988 — Gorbachev emphasised the right of each country to choose its own political and economic system, favouring trust and cooperation over confrontation; overall improved terms and relations with the US

While these reforms seemed great on paper, many did not work well when implemented. Gorbachev had hoped the newly reformed USSR would improve its economy and communist system; however, the plan backfired and the nation faced even greater issues, causing Soviet citizens to grow even more discontented with the government (as evident from frequent protests). This sped up the Soviet Union's eventual demise, as its citizens lost hope in the nation, the government and the communist cause, and looked to alternative governments and ideologies which could better benefit themselves and improve their lives.

topics.title: Eastern Europe: Prague Spring and the Fall of the Berlin Wall
topics.notesHtml:
Eastern Europe

Prague Spring (5th January 1968)

Context: Antonin Novotny, the Stalinist ruler of Czechoslovakia, was succeeded as First Secretary of the Czechoslovakian Communist Party by Alexander Dubcek, a Slovak who supported liberal reforms. In the first few months of his rule, Dubcek introduced a series of far-reaching political and economic reforms, including increased freedom of speech and the rehabilitation of political dissidents.

Effects: Dubcek's effort to establish "communism with a human face" was celebrated across the country, and the brief period of freedom became known as the Prague Spring. However, on 20 August 1968, the Soviet Union responded to Dubcek's reforms by invading Czechoslovakia with 600,000 Warsaw Pact troops. Prague was not eager to give way, but scattered student resistance was no match for Soviet tanks. Dubcek's reforms were repealed and he was replaced by the staunchly pro-Soviet Gustav Husak, who re-established an authoritarian communist regime in the country.

In 1989, as communist governments folded across Eastern Europe, Prague again became the scene of demonstrations for democratic reforms. In December 1989, Husak's government conceded to demands for a multiparty parliament.

Conclusion: The Prague Spring saw Czechoslovakian citizens gain more civil liberties following a nationwide liberalisation and move toward democracy. The USSR responded harshly to the crisis, but the citizens, having experienced the joys of civil liberties and a more democratic and liberal government, were prepared to reclaim their rights. The Spring was an obvious sign of the desire for freedom and democracy among communist subjects, and a general shift against communism, whether within or beyond communist states.

Fall of the Berlin Wall (9th November 1989)

Context: On 13 August 1961, the Communist government of the German Democratic Republic began to build a barbed wire and concrete "antifascist bulwark" between East and West Berlin. The official purpose of this Berlin Wall was to keep so-called Western "fascists" from entering East Germany and undermining the socialist state, but it primarily served to stem mass defections from East to West. The Berlin Wall also signified the divide between the communist and capitalist blocs, and stood until 9 November 1989, when the head of the East German Communist Party announced that citizens of the GDR could cross the border whenever they pleased. That night, ecstatic crowds swarmed the wall — some crossed freely into West Berlin, while others brought hammers and picks and began to chip away at the wall itself. To this day, the Berlin Wall remains one of the most powerful and enduring symbols of the Cold War.

Effects: The fall of the wall was a significant symbol, as the Berlin Wall symbolised the divide between communism and capitalism. Its fall implied that this divide had ceased to exist, and alluded to the fledgling communist ideology and eventual demise of the Soviet Union. With the collapse of the wall, East Berlin citizens could move freely into West Berlin and escape communism. Communism had weakened in Eastern Europe, dealing a major blow to the USSR and contributing to its collapse.

Conclusion: The fall of the Berlin Wall was a symbol of communism's end, freeing Europeans who had endured decades under communist rule. The removal of such a significant communist symbol signified the ideology's irrelevance and imminent death.

topics.title: Social Movements in Southeast Asia: Introduction
topics.notesHtml:
Social Movements in Southeast Asia

Social movements can be defined as loosely organized, purposeful groups striving to work towards a common goal. These movements can either create or resist change, providing a political voice to the disenfranchised. Unlike political movements, which aim to govern, social movements seek concessions from the state in the form of policy changes, protection or other forms of action.

Southeast Asia consists of the Buddhist-majority Indochina Peninsula and the Islam-majority maritime SEA. Both regions house many different ethnic and cultural groups. Due to its wealth in resources, religious influence, history of colonialism and wide spectrum of political systems, Southeast Asia has long been a hotbed for social changes:

  1. Politics of social and cultural change
    • Rapid social and cultural change in Southeast Asia has been afforded by power relations involved in the construction, functioning and transformation of cultural groups and societies
    • The negotiation of power between the dominant and subordinated in society, each with their own versions of reality and practice, is often articulated through struggles over particular cultural sites, e.g. struggles over heritage sites
  2. Constructing identities
    • Social groups emerge in relation to uneven political and economic arrangements wrought by processes such as globalization, migration and tourism, as well as how social and political institutions such as the family, paid employment and non-government organizations shape everyday lives and politics
  3. Social movements and influence
    • Social movements cannot exist without a considerable measure of democracy
    • Local social movements have been influenced by global social movement concerns and international discourse, e.g. war and environmental destruction, and causes such as civil rights, gender equality and the sexual revolution, shaped by funding and repertoires of action, and are able to leverage transnational networks to pursue local causes

This multitude of factors has led to the manifestation of social change in movements such as the Free Aceh Movement and the People Power Movement.

topics.title: Free Aceh Movement (GAM)
topics.notesHtml:
Free Aceh Movement

Aceh is a province located on the northern tip of Sumatra in the Indonesian Archipelago. In 1976, Acehnese intellectual Hasan di Tiro established the Free Aceh Movement (Gerakan Aceh Merdeka; GAM) — a separatist group which sought the independence of Aceh from Indonesia. The insurgency, known to the central government as the Aceh Security Disturbance Movement (GPK), pursued its goals mainly through armed struggle with the Indonesian Army, lasting through the 1990s. In 2005, after a deadly tsunami devastated the region, a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) was signed, resulting in GAM giving up its arms and goals of independence in exchange for political power.

Driving Forces

Political:

  1. Fight for self-determination and the Acehnese identity:
    • Under the Sukarno government, they were promised special benefits and their own land, but were incorporated under North Sumatra in 1950 and lacked autonomy
    • After the Darul Islam rebellion in the 1950s, they were promised special territory status, but still lacked power to make decisions for themselves
    • Suharto's 'New Order' in 1966 centralised power, causing political alienation of Aceh (little provincial power)
  2. Human rights abuses:
    • Oppressed political voice — could not speak up about the violence occurring
    • Operational Military Status (DOM) declared in 1991, leading to about 2,000 people being killed in the first 3 years of operations (1989-1992)
    • Families who supported Aceh Merdeka were sometimes arrested without reason

Social:

  1. Social identity:
    • Historical roots as a powerful Islamic state
    • Resistance to Dutch colonial rule (Aceh War: 1873-1942)
    • Belief that they are a superior race, culturally distinct from the Javanese
    • Compared to the secular government, wanted to establish an independent Islamic state under Sharia Law
    • Political Islam was suppressed under Suharto
  2. Social tensions:
    • Indonesia's transmigration policy led to many Javanese being displaced to the Aceh mountains and industrial coasts
    • Due to tension between Javanese and Acehnese, the Acehnese could not go to the mountains or coastal zones, and were suffocating in the middle
    • Immoral activities occurred, e.g. trafficking, cannabis cultivation and sexual assaults

Religious:

  1. Strict adherence to Islam and religious identity:
    • Had to safeguard this strong religious identity
    • Threatened by the Sukarno Indonesian government's practices of secularism
    • Wanted to turn Indonesia into an Islamic state
    • Disagreements over the implementation of Islamic (Sharia) laws in the national government

Economic:

  1. Exploitation of Aceh's resources:
    • Aceh, rich in natural liquid gas and petroleum, is accountable for 15% of Indonesia's exports
    • Acehnese lived in poverty while the Javanese exploited their resources
    • Many Acehnese were disadvantaged by industrial development projects in Aceh, which provided employment opportunities to the Javanese instead
    • Wanted independence so the Acehnese could reap their own benefits
  2. Recession in 1997:
    • Aceh's GDP declined 5.9% in 1998, then a further 2.9% in 1999
    • Believed that independence would boost its economy

Impacts

Political Impact:

  1. Insignificant national impact:
    • Aceh is only 2% of the national population
    • The international community did not want to spoil ties with Indonesia over Aceh

Aceh is only a very small part of Indonesia, insignificant in terms of population, land area, or the natural resources and economy it contributes to the central government. Thus, Indonesia did not make significant responses to GAM and largely let it be. Moreover, calls by GAM leaders for support from other parties like the US were often ignored, as those nations and the general international community wanted to maintain good ties with Indonesia. Therefore, at the national and international level, little was done in response to the movement, resulting in largely insignificant and unremarkable impacts.

  1. Local political successes:
    • Irwandi Yusuf, a prominent GAM figure, won the governorship
    • GAM won 33/69 seats in Aceh's regional parliament
    • GAM won 10/23 seats in municipal offices
    • GAM turned into a legitimate political party called the Aceh Party after the Memorandum of Understanding in Helsinki

At the local and provincial level, there were significant changes to GAM's operations. GAM transformed from a violent organisation seeking power through fighting and clashing with Indonesian forces, into a political organization seeking power through legal means by participating in politics. Former rebels became politicians and gained power via elections, allowing them to draft policies and enact laws geared towards benefiting the Acehnese. The movement thus became a peaceful and effective one.

  1. Demilitarisation:
    • Many former GAM members gained prestigious political seats
    • Cessation of armed conflict and a ceasefire

Social Impact:

  1. Islamic State established:
    • In 2006, Aceh was legally allowed to implement Sharia Law, making Islamic Law the legal law in Aceh
    • Shows they are a step closer towards independence and establishing an Islamic state
  2. Human rights loopholes:
    • A Human Rights Justice court faced many problems before it could even be established
    • Multiple human rights violations continued

Economic Impact:

  1. Economic opportunities opened up:
    • Economic control over its own ports and exports
    • 70% revenue share for natural gas and oil exports
  2. Negative impacts:
    • US$4.4 billion in losses during the earthquake/tsunami in 2005, requiring reliance on Indonesia
    • A quarter of the population still lives below the poverty line

Overview

  1. Separatist group seeking independence for the Aceh region of Sumatra
  2. From 1976 to 2005, with a peace process unfolding until 2009
  3. Ceasefire happened after the 2004 tsunami, and the group dissolved its military with a peace agreement; former GAM leaders joined local government

Key Events Timeline

  1. 1945 — Indonesia declares independence; Aceh is incorporated into the province of North Sumatra
  2. 1950-1959 — Darul Islam Rebellion in Aceh; central government reaches a special autonomy agreement in 1959
  3. 1966 — President Suharto implements the New Order Indonesia, centralising power with the government
  4. 1976 — Hasan di Tiro declares independence for Aceh
  5. 1979 — Initial rebellion is crushed; GAM leaders flee to Europe and set up a government-in-exile
  6. 1989 — Libyan-trained GAM fighters enter Aceh and conduct military operations
  7. 1990-1998 — President Suharto declares Aceh a special military zone; 6,000 additional security forces are moved to Aceh; GAM resistance is largely destroyed
  8. 1998 — President Suharto is made to resign due to the economic crisis
  9. 1999 — GAM resumes military and civil activity; East Timor holds an independence referendum; an Aceh Independence rally is held in Banda Aceh, with some estimates placing 1 million participants there
  10. 1999-2004 — Despite suffering heavy losses at the hands of the Indonesian military, GAM is still able to operate; military stalemate
  11. 2004 — Boxing Day tsunami; ceasefire declared
  12. 2005 — Helsinki Memorandum of Understanding; GAM's military arm disarmed; Indonesia withdraws troops and releases prisoners
  13. 2006/2007 — GAM representative Irwandi Yusuf wins election for Governor of Aceh
  14. 2009 — GAM political candidates win 33/69 seats in Aceh's regional parliament and 10/23 seats in municipal offices

topics.title: People Power Movement (Philippines)
topics.notesHtml:
People Power Movement (Philippines)

Reasons/Driving Forces

Political:

  1. Corrupt Marcos government:
    • Martial Law declared in 1972 to keep Marcos in power
    • A new constitution allowed Marcos to rule for 14 years instead of two (facilitated further by the rigged snap elections of 1986)
    • 3,200 known killings and 35,000 documented cases of torture under the authoritarian Marcos regime
    • Former Senator Benigno "Ninoy" Aquino Sr, one of Marcos' main political enemies, was shot and killed at the airport in 1983
  2. Call for reform:
    • Lack of freedom, oppression, living in a climate of fear
    • Unable to carry out democratic elections and choose their own government
    • Heavy political corruption

Social:

  1. United society (civil):
    • Over 2 million people condemned Marcos and launched the "Triumph for the People" campaign of civil disobedience
    • All had a common goal of overthrowing the Marcos government
  2. Access to mass media:
    • Celebrities and churches alike joined the movement, making it widespread
    • The Catholic radio station, Radio Veritas, became a major control centre for the People Power movement's communications

Economic:

  1. Economic recession:
    • 1980s economic collapse brought about by extravagant spending in the 1960s and over-reliance on debt
    • Economy contracted by 7.3% over the following 2 years
    • The peso lost about 80% of its value
    • By 1982, the Philippines' debt was about $24.4 billion

Religious:

  1. Involvement of the Catholic Church:
    • The Catholic Church's support led to mass mobilization, with many churches calling for followers to demonstrate and support the movement

Impacts

Political achievements:

  1. Short-term democratic reforms:
    • 1987 Constitutional Reform removed and changed many repressive laws, shifting from a regimentary to a parliamentary system
    • Intended to strengthen democracy and freedom for the people
    • Power was split into 3 arms of government: executive, legislative and judicial
  2. Cannot sustain political achievements:
    • Cases of political corruption continued to occur
    • Some of Aquino's promises were not kept, such as the dismantling of US Army bases in the Philippines

Social and civil successes:

  1. Legacy of the People Power Movement:
    • Other movements were inspired by the effectiveness of the People Power Movement, e.g. the Arab Spring (2010), Hong Kong protests (2019) and the Burmese Civil Disobedience Movement (2021)

Economic benefit:

  1. Recovery efforts for the economy:
    • The economy made small growth during Aquino's presidency (3.4% on average)
    • President Aquino paid off $4 billion of debt incurred under the Marcos government, but continued to borrow to fund infrastructure development, upholding the Philippines' economic credibility
    • Reduced the debt-to-GDP ratio by 30%
    • No major economic growth was noted, but a lot of clean-up work was needed after the Marcos government had shattered the economy

shortAnswer.prompt: Compare the political achievements of the People Power Movement with those of the Free Aceh Movement in the years following each movement's peak.
shortAnswer.modelAnswer: Both movements achieved genuine political transformation but of different kinds. The People Power Movement resulted in swift, nationwide constitutional reform in 1987, restructuring the entire Philippine government into three arms and removing repressive laws almost immediately after Marcos's fall. The Free Aceh Movement's political success, by contrast, was more gradual and localised: after the 2005 MoU, GAM transformed into a legal political party, eventually winning provincial parliamentary seats and the governorship years later, without nationwide constitutional change. This shows that while both movements achieved lasting institutional change, People Power produced immediate national-level reform whereas Aceh's success was slower and confined mainly to the regional level.

topics.title: Urbanisation: The Growth of Cities and USA Urbanisation (19th-20th Century)
topics.notesHtml:
Urbanisation

The Growth of Cities

The industrial revolution of the 19th and 20th centuries transformed urban life, giving people high expectations for improving their standard of living, and its developments encouraged migration to cities:

  • Improved transportation moved goods and people quickly and easily
  • Industrialization allowed for more goods to be produced cheaply by machines
  • Commercialisation allowed for the production of goods for a mass market, meeting high demand from the people

USA Urbanisation, 19th-20th Century

Reasons

  1. Technological Advancement:
    • Rise in the number of cars and the motor industry: facilitated immigration and urbanisation; created greater employment in the motor and manufacturing industries; eased transportation, allowing city boundaries to expand as workers could travel beyond walking-distance commutes
    • Communication technology, particularly the development of telephones: eased communication, boosting efficiency and helping fuel the rise of larger national companies and corporations
    • Long-distance transportation: rail and ships facilitated international immigration, especially from Europe given the context of WWI and WWII, as people escaped war and religious persecution
  2. Immigration Push and Pull Factors:
    • Push factors: religious persecution (e.g. of Eastern European Jews during the European wars); poverty and conflict (WWI, WWII, Korean War); poor working and living conditions (e.g. the Great Irish Potato Famine of 1845)
    • Pull factors: economic opportunities — a safe haven with high demand for labour and financial/economic security
    • Political factors: laws from the United States (a country built by immigrants); immigration quotas
  3. Economic Opportunities:
    • New products and new means of production (e.g. assembly line manufacturing) meant new industries formed and old industries flourished
    • Workers were attracted by jobs and higher wages
    • High employment meant more labour was needed: in 1929, the auto industry employed 500,000 workers; in 1921, 12% of Americans were unemployed, so more rural residents decided to move to urban areas in search of employment
    • Dense city populations attracted business, with stores moving to cities (agglomeration economics)
    • WWI and WWII: the USA supplied the European war effort
    • Given the reduced economic significance of the farming industry in the 1920s, more rural farmers moved to cities in search of employment

Effects

  1. Growth of cities
  2. City planning
  3. Movement of people
  4. Rising income gaps

Impacts

Social:

  • Overpopulation:
    • Shortage of social services provision, e.g. healthcare services
    • Lack of food and housing — high rents, low wages and poor services produced misery in the midst of unprecedented economic growth
    • The growth of cities outpaced the ability of local governments to extend clean water, garbage collection and sewage systems into poorer areas, so conditions in cities deteriorated
  • Social unrest: rise in crime rates
  • Social segregation — creation of inner and outer cities:
    • The wealthy created separate neighbourhoods for themselves by building mansions on large plots of land at the edges of cities or in the countryside, catering mainly to the new middle class of white-collar employees in business and industry
    • Poorer people — newcomers from the countryside and immigrants — moved into the old housing stock
    • Landlords took advantage of the demand for housing by subdividing city houses into apartments and building tenements, which are low-rent apartment buildings that were often poorly maintained and unsanitary

Political: Political corruption was rampant in city government and city services, especially in the construction industry and among landlords and employers.

Economic: Unemployment increased due to greater competition.

Environmental: Pollution and environmental degradation.
